paper_design_summary: Two online controlled experiments recruited Prolific participants: the math study analyzed 315 people under no assistance, tutor, peer-agent, or tutor-plus-peer conditions, and the writing study analyzed 247 people writing creative and argumentative essays with no assistant, one generalist, or a pair of specialized assistants (pp. 3-6 and 8, Sections 3.1 and 4.1). Math was tested after assistance was removed; writing was scored by an LLM quality rubric and by embedding similarity across writers while assistance was available (pp. 4, 6-8, Sections 3.1.4, 4.1.3-4.1.4 and 4.2). The saved document does not explicitly state random assignment to the assistance conditions, so the writing study's core eligibility remains unclear.

studies.label: Experiment-1: Math Problem-Solving with LLM Tutor and Peers

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants worked under Control, Tutor Only, Peers Only, or Tutor + Peers. Random assignment of people to these support conditions is not stated. Random topic selection and random selection of a responding peer are described, but do not establish randomized assistance assignment. This is an online controlled experiment with an unspecified allocation method.
assignment.quote: participants were introduced to the task and to the agents assigned to their condition (where applicable).
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 2, Section 3 and footnote 1: https://aspredicted.org/rq8uz9.pdf; p. 4, Sections 3.1.5 and 3.2.1. The linked registration could not be retrieved because network access was denied.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: No agents, chat interface, or feedback; participants moved directly to the next question instead of an agent lesson (pp. 3-4, Sections 3.1.2 and 3.1.4).

arms.name: Tutor Only
arms.description: Bob, a GPT-5.2 tutor, provided feedback, hints and follow-up questions (pp. 2-3, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2).

arms.name: Peers Only
arms.description: Two GPT-5.2 peer agents: Alice makes arithmetic errors and Charlie makes conceptual errors; they discuss alternative solutions with the participant (p. 3, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.2).

arms.name: Tutor + Peers
arms.description: Bob, Alice and Charlie were all present; the tutor provided feedback to the participant and peer agents and guided follow-up discussion (p. 3, Section 3.1.2).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 614 recruited and 315 passing the preregistered attention and authenticity checks; the latter are the analyzed sample. It does not print a separate excluded count, a count at randomized assignment, or arm-specific participant counts (p. 4, Section 3.1.5).
participants.who: English-fluent Prolific workers with an approval rating of at least 99% and at least 100 completed platform tasks (p. 4, Section 3.1.5).
participants.quote: Following our preregistered exclusion criteria, only 315 participants passed our attention and authenticity checks

ai_tool.how_used: Role-prompted tutor and peer agents participated in a free-form lesson chat. Participants could intervene with questions or reasoning. Tutor Bob used clarifications, hints and encouragement; the peers presented intentionally error-prone solutions. AI was removed for the scored test (pp. 2-4, Sections 3.1.1-3.1.4).

task.description: SAT-level mathematical problem solving, not a creativity or ideation task. Each participant studied two sampled problem categories and then answered their isomorphic variants without AI. The primary score is mathematical test accuracy; it is outside the creativity codebook and is not entered as a creativity outcome (p. 4, Sections 3.1.3-3.1.4).
task.duration: A 5-minute agent lesson per problem, followed by a 1-minute Tetris distractor before the unassisted test; the task took approximately 14 minutes. Control skipped the agent lessons (p. 4, Sections 3.1.4-3.1.5).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants worked in a three-condition between-subjects design: Control, Single, or Duo. The text does not say these support conditions were randomly assigned. It explicitly randomizes writing prompts, essay order, the model used within Single, and the model-to-role mapping within Duo. Those randomizations do not establish random assignment to Control, Single and Duo. Coded other because the document establishes neither an RCT nor explicitly non-random assistance assignment.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 4 and Sections 4.1.1-4.1.2; p. 6, Section 4.1.3
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 5, Section 4, footnote 2: https://aspredicted.org/gq922f.pdf; p. 8, Section 4.1.5 refers to pre-registered exclusion criteria. The registration itself could not be retrieved because network access was denied.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Participants wrote without AI assistance (p. 5, Section 4).

arms.name: Single
arms.description: One generalist writing assistant, randomly selected within this condition as Claude Opus 4.6 or ChatGPT GPT-5.2, providing concise feedback on the developing essay (p. 5, Section 4.1.2).

arms.name: Duo
arms.description: Both Claude Opus 4.6 and ChatGPT GPT-5.2, assigned complementary writing roles. Creative roles emphasize imagination/voice versus craft/structure; argumentative roles emphasize dialectic versus logic/evidence. Model-to-role assignment is randomized (p. 5, Section 4.1.2).

participants.exclusions: 419 recruited; 247 produced two usable essays after the preregistered attention check and a minimum of 40 words in both essays. The paper reports approximately 41% attrition. These are analyzed participants, not a stated count at assignment; arm-specific counts and an explicit excluded count are absent (p. 8, Section 4.1.5).
participants.who: English-fluent Prolific workers with an approval rating of at least 99% and at least 100 completed platform tasks (p. 8, Section 4.1.5).
participants.quote: 247 of the 419 recruited participants produced two usable essays

ai_tool.how_used: Assistants read the current essay text and offered feedback during writing; participants could initiate questions and free-form discussion throughout. Single was a generalist with feedback limited to 50 words per message. Duo used complementary role-specific feedback and was instructed to build on the other agent's comments (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.1.2-4.1.3). The primary function is feedback on developing writing; open chat was also available.

task.description: Each participant wrote an argumentative essay and a creative essay, approximately 200-300 words each, with one prompt randomly selected from a pool of 3 per essay type and randomized essay order. Prompts were drawn from the New York Times Student Opinion series. Assigned assistance remained available during production of the scored essays; there is no later unassisted writing assessment (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.3; p. 10, Section 5.2).
task.duration: Section 4.1.1 says at least 5 minutes per essay (p. 5), whereas Section 4.1.3 says a 5-minute time limit (p. 6). Median total completion time was 11 minutes (p. 8, Section 4.1.5).

outcomes.name: Combined essay quality (creative and argumentative)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-5.2 rated each essay on rubric dimensions using a 1-5 scale. The creative rubric covers originality, narrative structure/coherence, elaboration/richness, expressiveness/emotional impact, and literary quality/language use; the argumentative rubric covers clarity, evidence/reasoning, organization, counterarguments, persuasiveness, and language/formality. Section 4.1.4 says dimension ratings are summed per essay; Section 4.2.1 and Figure 7a describe the analyzed combined score as the average of the two essay scores on a 1-5 scale. The conversion from rubric sums to that scale is not explained. Coded as quality/usefulness, with originality among its components. Human ratings validate the automated measure only: two independent raters scored 83 essays (49 creative, 34 argumentative), Pearson r = .87; human-GPT Spearman rho = .77 for creative and .73 for argumentative. These are essays and reliability statistics, not additional participants or treatment effects (pp. 6-7, Section 4.1.4; p. 7, Figure 7a; p. 8, Section 4.2.1).

contrasts.reported: Control vs. Single: Δ = 0.332, t(244) = 6.21, p < .0001; planned comparison with Bonferroni correction. The paper describes Single as higher quality. Overall condition model: F(2, 244) = 21.91, p < .0001, R² = 0.152. Arm means, SDs, numerical SEs, and standardized effects are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.2.1 Essay quality; p. 7, Figure 7a

contrasts.reported: Control vs. Duo: Δ = 0.234, t(244) = 4.21, p = 0.0001; planned comparison with Bonferroni correction. The paper describes Duo as higher quality.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.2.1 Essay quality; p. 7, Figure 7a

contrasts.reported: Single vs. Duo (paper's printed contrast order): Δ = 0.098, t(244) = 1.56, p = 0.363; planned comparison with Bonferroni correction. These printed numbers refer to Single versus Duo; they have not been sign-reversed or recomputed for the listed Duo treatment arm.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.2.1 Essay quality; p. 7, Figure 7a

outcomes.name: Idea-level diversity across writers (key-point cosine similarity)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: gpt-5-mini extracted 3-5 atomic key points per essay: distinct claims for argumentative essays and narrative elements or themes for creative essays. SBERT embeddings were used to compute mean pairwise cosine similarity within condition-by-prompt cells, with resampling to equalize cell sizes and aggregation across prompts. Higher raw similarity means less diversity. No separate effects by essay type or prompt are printed (p. 7, Section 4.1.4; p. 8, Section 4.2.2).

contrasts.reported: Mean similarity: Single: 0.748 vs. Control: 0.735; permutation p = .033. The direction is reversed for diversity: higher similarity means lower diversity. Arm similarity means are printed, but SDs, arm participant counts, numerical SEs and interval bounds are not.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.2.2 Idea-level diversity; p. 7, Figure 7b

contrasts.reported: Mean similarity: Duo: 0.737 vs. Control: 0.735; p = .950. Higher similarity means lower diversity; the paper reports no detectable difference.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.2.2 Idea-level diversity; p. 7, Figure 7b

contrasts.reported: Mean similarity: Duo: 0.737; Single: 0.748. Duo vs. Single: p = .065. The observed lower similarity favors diversity with Duo, but the pairwise comparison does not establish a clear difference at the conventional threshold.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.2.2 Idea-level diversity; p. 7, Figure 7b

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of SBERT embeddings of LLM-extracted essay key points; higher similarity means greater homogenization.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence transformer (SBERT); exact checkpoint not stated (p. 7, Section 4.1.4).
diversity_detail.computed_over: All key points from essays in a condition-by-prompt cell after sampling essays with replacement, then averaged across prompts within a condition. The paper describes similarity across essays, but does not explicitly state whether pairs of key points from the same essay are excluded (p. 7, Section 4.1.4).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Per condition-by-prompt cell, sample n = 15 essays with replacement for M = 1,000 rounds to obtain a mean and 95% confidence interval. For each pair of conditions, pool their essays, shuffle condition labels, and recompute differences in mean bootstrapped similarity for M = 1,000 permutations; two-sided p is based on differences at least as large in magnitude. Resampling and label permutation are described at the essay level; participant-level clustering is not described (p. 7, Section 4.1.4).
diversity_detail.notes: Figure 7 says error bars are +/-1 SEM, while the methods describe bootstrap 95% confidence intervals; numerical uncertainty bounds are not printed. The bootstrap n = 15 is not the participant count, and the number of key points or pairs is not reported. Direction codes use diversity, while reported numbers preserve the paper's similarity scale (p. 7, Figure 7 and Section 4.1.4).

company_involvement.description: No company affiliation, funding, or study involvement is disclosed. All authors are affiliated with the University of Toronto; acknowledgments name help with graphics and discussions.

eligibility.reason: Experiment-2 meets the people threshold with 247 analyzed participants (p. 8, Section 4.1.5) and measures essay quality and cross-writer idea diversity on produced output (pp. 6-8, Sections 4.1.4 and 4.2.1-4.2.2; p. 7, Figure 7). However, the three assistance conditions are described only as a between-subjects design; explicitly randomized prompts, task order, models within Single, and model-role mappings within Duo do not establish random assistance assignment (pp. 5-6, Sections 4-4.1.3). The linked preregistration could not be retrieved. Design is coded other pending allocation verification, rather than assuming either an RCT or non-random observational allocation. Experiment-1 has 315 analyzed participants but ordinary SAT-level math accuracy is outside the creativity task scope (p. 4, Sections 3.1.3-3.1.5).

one_line_finding: Among 247 analyzed writers, Single and Duo improved quality versus Control (Δ = 0.332 and 0.234), Single increased idea similarity (0.748 vs. 0.735; p = .033), and the Duo-Single similarity comparison was inconclusive (p = .065; p. 8, Sections 4.1.5 and 4.2.1-4.2.2).
open_questions: Were participants randomly assigned to the main assistance conditions in either experiment? Neither the saved PDF nor its full markdown states this explicitly. The linked preregistrations could not be accessed (pp. 2-6, Sections 3-4.1.3).
What are the numbers assigned and analyzed in each arm, and were all assigned participants included? Only recruited and retained totals are provided (p. 4, Section 3.1.5; p. 8, Section 4.1.5).
Where is the Appendix mentioned for system prompts, and does it contain additional information about allocation or analyses? It is absent from the saved PDF (p. 2, Section 3.1.1; PDF ends on p. 12).
How were the per-essay sums described in the methods converted to the reported combined 1-5 quality score (p. 6, Section 4.1.4; p. 7, Figure 7a; p. 8, Section 4.2.1)?

Which SBERT checkpoint was used, were within-essay key-point pairs excluded, and did resampling/permutation account for each person contributing both essay types? Were the plotted diversity bars SEM or bootstrap confidence intervals (p. 7, Section 4.1.4 and Figure 7)?
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. Read the complete markdown, including all references; the conversion contains no appendix. Checked the PDF text for the title/version, methods, participant counts, Figure 7, and every numerical result entered. Both studies are retained as study entries, but ordinary math test accuracy and all self-reported perceptions are outside the creativity outcomes inventory. Math testing occurred after AI removal; writing outcomes were produced with assistance available in the AI arms. Following the form requirement to list every scored output outcome, the eleven explicitly rated rubric dimensions are recorded with empty contrasts because separate results are absent; together with combined essay quality and diversity this gives thirteen outcome entries. The creative and argumentative composite scores are components of the combined-quality endpoint and are described there. No participant totals were inferred from essay counts, no arm counts were reconstructed, and no effect sizes or SEs were computed. Diversity p_value_only denotes the available inferential statistic; the printed similarity means are preserved in reported. No participant reuse or reanalysis is stated; no study-specific data/code URL is given. The paper's 562 in the abstract is a cross-experiment total, not the sample size of either study (p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Section 3.1.5; p. 8, Section 4.1.5). Requests for both named preregistration PDFs used urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1 without personal identifiers, but failed with WinError 10013; no external material was saved or used.
